extracted.intended_audience: writers, editors, copyeditors, and publishers using Chicago style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines from the Chicago Manual of Style on how to present numbers, dates, times, units, currencies, and numbered references in nontechnical and technical prose. Includes consistency rules, SI and ISO recommendations, punctuation, and special cases (eras, centuries, telephone numbers, inclusive ranges, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize 'n' in 'nth degree'
rubrics_metrics.description: In the expression “nth degree,” Chicago style is to italicize the n (see also 7.64).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and flexibility in numeric presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where many numbers occur within a paragraph or a series of paragraphs, maintain consistency in the immediate context: if by rule you must use numerals for one of the numbers in a given category, use them for all in that category; an exception may be made at the beginning of a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An exception may be made to avoid a thickly clustered group of spelled-out numbers; in some cases the exception may apply to a passage or a work as a whole (e.g., all ages in a book given as numerals). See also rules cited (e.g., 9.5, 9.2, 9.4, 9.8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative rule for small numbers in context
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative rule allows certain small numbers (examples given: 13–18 spelled as numerals in a list of ages, with smaller ones spelled out) to be treated differently depending on context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use editorial discretion to follow alternative rule examples; consult related sections (9.3, 9.7) for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid thickly clustered spelled-out numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: An exception to the general or alternative rule may be made to avoid a thickly clustered group of spelled-out numbers, regardless of category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exception can be applied within a paragraph, passage, or the whole work for consistency/readability (example: many ages in a book rendered as numerals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Large numbers with million/billion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whole numbers used in combination with million, billion, and so forth usually follow the general rule (see 9.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For monetary amounts, see 9.20–25; for scientific superscripts see 9.9. Examples: 'from three million in 1960 to fourteen million in 1990'; fractional millions mix numerals and words for readability ('2.3 million'). Note country differences in meaning of 'billion' and higher prefixes; query writers unfamiliar with American usage (see 5.250 under billion; trillion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific notation and powers of ten
rubrics_metrics.description: Large round numbers may be expressed in powers of ten (scientific notation) especially in scientific writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and conversions provided (10^2 = 100, 5.34 x 10^8 = 534,000,000). Consult Scientific Style and Format for further examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: SI prefixes (mega-, giga-, tera-, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: According to SI, very large quantities may be indicated by prefixes such as mega- (million), giga- (billion), tera- (trillion) as part of the unit; inversely, milli-, micro-, nano- for small quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These expressions often use symbols (M for mega- as in MB). In astrophysics, Myr and Gyr (megayear, gigayear) are sometimes used. See 10.56 for a complete list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary multiples vs SI prefixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Note that terms such as megabyte, when used as binary multiples, are approximations—a megabyte was originally equal to 1,048,576 bytes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current SI usage dictates that such prefixes refer to powers of ten; for binary multiples use the first two letters of the prefix plus 'bi' (kibibyte, mebibyte, gibibyte). See also 9.11–9.14.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'dex' as decimal exponent shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'dex' is sometimes used in scientific notation as shorthand for decimal exponent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that errors of 3 dex (i.e., 10^3) can lead to dangerous misconceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical quantities in nontechnical contexts follow general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: In nontechnical material, physical quantities such as distances, lengths, areas, and so on are usually treated according to the general rule (see 9.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Within fifteen minutes the temperature dropped twenty degrees.' Certain commonly expressed quantities (size, wattage, inch measurements, miles per gallon) may be set as numerals by editorial discretion but must be applied consistently across like quantities (see examples: 'a 40-watt bulb', 'a size 14 dress', 'a 32-inch inseam', 'a fuel efficiency of 80 miles per gallon'). See also 9.7.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple fractions spelled out and hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple fractions are spelled out and, for readability and consistency, are hyphenated in noun, adjective, and adverb forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'She has read three-fourths of the book.' If an individual part is emphasized, the expression may be unhyphenated ('three quarters'). See 7.89 for hyphenation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whole numbers plus fractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantities consisting of whole numbers and simple fractions may be spelled out if short but are often better expressed in numerals, especially if a symbol for the fraction is available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'We walked for three and one-quarter (or three and a quarter) miles.' Use numerals when readability requires it ('Lester is exactly 3 feet 5½ inches tall'). See 9.17, 10.66.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use numerals with abbreviations and symbols for units
rubrics_metrics.description: If an abbreviation or a symbol is used for the unit of measure, the quantity is always expressed by a numeral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is standard in mathematical, statistical, technical, and scientific text. No hyphen between numeral and abbreviation/symbol; normally include a space between numeral and unit (exceptions: degree, percent, prime symbols). Examples: '50 km (kilometers); a 50 km race; 240 V; 10°C; 45 L; 85 g.' A unit used without a numeral should be spelled out ('kilojoules', not 'kj'). See 10.49–68.

rubrics_metrics.name: Units for repeated quantities repeat abbreviation when closed up
rubrics_metrics.description: For expressions including two or more quantities, the abbreviation or symbol is repeated if it is closed up to the number but not if it is separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '35%-50%' and '3°C-7°C' (symbols repeated); '6" x 9"' vs '2 x 5 cm' (when separated, repetition may not be needed). See 10.49 and 10.58 for spacing rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentages usually expressed in numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Except at the beginning of a sentence, percentages are usually expressed in numerals. In nontechnical contexts use the word 'percent'; in scientific/statistical copy the symbol '%' is more common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Fewer than 3 percent...', 'With 90-95 percent of the work complete...' Note: percent (adverb) is not interchangeable with percentage (noun). No space between numeral and '%' symbol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decimal fractions and use of leading zero
rubrics_metrics.description: Large or complex fractions are expressed as numeric decimal fractions. When a quantity equals less than 1.00, a zero normally appears before the decimal point as an aid to readability, particularly in scientific contexts and when quantities >1 appear in the same context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a mean of 0.73', 'the ratio 0.85'. In contexts where decimal quantities must be ≤1.00 (probabilities, batting averages, correlation coefficients), the leading zero is typically omitted (e.g., '.367'). See 9.19.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money: words vs symbols and numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolated references to amounts of money are spelled out for whole numbers of one hundred or less, following the general principle (see 9.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'seventy-five cents = 75¢', 'fifteen dollars = $15'. Whole amounts expressed numerically should include zeros and a decimal point only when they appear in the same context with fractional amounts ('Prices ranged from $0.95 up to $10.00'). See 9.20–25 for larger amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify non-US currencies when $ is ambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: In contexts where the symbol $ may refer to non‑US currencies, these currencies should be clearly identified (e.g., C$300, NZ$749).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ISO three-letter currency codes (USD, CAD, NZD, AUD, MXN, etc.) may be more appropriate in formal usage. See ISO 4217 and 9.24.

rubrics_metrics.name: British and other currencies formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: British currency: basic unit is the pound (£), one-hundredth is the penny (p). Most other currencies are handled like US currency with decimal point between main unit and subunits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'fifteen pounds = £15', 'fifty pence = 50p', 'forty euros = €40 (or EUR 40)'. Pre-euro historical currencies noted; use ISO codes where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large monetary amounts use numerals or mixed forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Sums of money of more than one hundred dollars are normally expressed by numerals; numbers of a million or more often use a mixture of numerals and spelled-out words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '$1,000', '$250 million', '$7.3 billion'. In some financial contexts thousands may be represented by 'K' (e.g., $350K).

rubrics_metrics.name: Currency with dates
rubrics_metrics.description: When the value of a currency in a particular year matters, insert the date in parentheses after the currency symbol (no intervening space).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'US$(1992)2.47' or better 'USD (1992) 2.47' when letters are used (spaces inserted). See 9.23–9.24.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers for page/chapter/volume/table references
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers referring to pages, chapters, parts, volumes, illustrations, or tables are set as numerals; front matter pages usually lowercase roman numerals and the rest arabic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For en dashes with number ranges see 6.78; consult chapters 14 and 15 for documentation style and 8.180 for other guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biblical references in numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Biblical references are given in numerals only; chapter and verse are separated by a colon with no space following it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Acts 27:1', '2 Corinthians 11:29-30'. For abbreviations see 10.44–48.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbered divisions in legal instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Arabic or roman numerals commonly distinguish divisions within legal instruments; when in doubt, prefer arabic numerals or consult the document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mixture of arabic and roman sometimes distinguishes smaller from larger divisions. See 14.269–305 for legal citation style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Years in numerals unless sentence-beginning
rubrics_metrics.description: Years are expressed in numerals unless they stand at the beginning of a sentence (in which case rewording may be preferable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'We all know what happened in 1776.' 'Records for solar eclipses go back at least as far as 3000 BCE.' Avoid beginning a sentence with a bare year.

rubrics_metrics.name: All-numeral dates discouraged in formal writing
rubrics_metrics.description: All‑numeral styles of writing dates (e.g., 5/10/99 or 5.10.99) should not be used in formal writing except for well-known brief forms (9/11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When quoting ambiguous all-numeral dates, ascertain and clarify month-day order. In text spell out full date; in tables with many dates, abbreviate months and consider day-month-year form (e.g., 5 Oct 2003).

rubrics_metrics.name: ISO date style (YYYY-MM-DD)
rubrics_metrics.description: ISO recommends an all‑numeral year-month-day style with hyphens; year given in full and one‑digit month/day preceded by zero (e.g., 2018-07-14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ISO style allows machine-sortable dates and is recommended for technical contexts; see 9.36 and 9.40.

rubrics_metrics.name: Times of day: words vs numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Times in even, half, and quarter hours are usually spelled out in text (with o'clock always spelled out); numerals are used when exact times are emphasized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples spelled out: 'five o'clock', 'half past three'. Examples numerals: 'The first train leaves at 5:22 a.m.' Chicago recommends lowercase 'a.m.' and 'p.m.' and advises not to use them with 'morning/afternoon/evening/night' or 'o'clock'. See 9.38–9.40.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noon and midnight spelled out (avoid 12:00 p.m./a.m.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers should never be used to express noon or midnight in general prose (except informally). '12:00 p.m.' is ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'noon' and 'midnight'; for double-date clarity use both dates when birth/death spans midnight (example given). See 9.40.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-four-hour system and ISO time style
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 24-hour system, four digits normally appear (often with no punctuation); ISO recommends 24-hour time with colons between hours, minutes, and seconds in running text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '14:38 = 2:38 p.m.' '2018-07-14 16:09:41.3' for combined ISO date/time. Military/scientific contexts may write '1500 hours' or '1500h'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerals for monarchs, popes, and ordinals after names
rubrics_metrics.description: Sovereigns, emperors, popes, and Orthodox patriarchs with the same name are differentiated by numerals, traditionally roman (e.g., Elizabeth II, Benedict XVI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In English contexts use the roman numeral alone; continental practice may add a period or superscript. For personal names with ordinals, no punctuation precedes the numeral unless the name is inverted (index entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers for sequels and quoted titles follow source usage
rubrics_metrics.description: When referring to sequels (books, movies) or quoted titles that use numerals or spelled-out numbers, follow the usage reflected in the source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The Godfather, Part II'; 'Jaws 2'; quote original punctuation/spelling even if unconventional ('Dumb and Dumber To [sic]').

rubrics_metrics.name: Vehicle/vessel and spacecraft numbering conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Boats and similar craft usually take a roman numeral; spacecraft usually an arabic numeral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Bluebird III' (boat) vs 'Mariner 9' (spacecraft). See 8.116–18 for further context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out ordinals designating successive governments/units when ≤100
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinal numbers designating successive dynasties, governments, political/judicial divisions, military units, and places of worship are spelled out if one hundred or less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Eighteenth Dynasty', 'Second International', 'Fifth Ward', 'Fourth Infantry Division', 'Fourth Presbyterian Church'. See related sections for specifics (8.51, 8.62, 8.71, 8.112).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unions, lodges, and similar local branch numbers as arabic numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers designating local branches of labor unions and fraternal lodges are usually expressed in arabic numerals after the name, with commas often omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Chicago Typographical Union No. 16', 'United Auto Workers Local 890', 'American Legion Post 21'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbered highways and streets formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: State, federal, and interstate highways are designated by arabic numerals (US Route 41, Interstate 90). Numbered streets and avenues are usually spelled out if one hundred or less ('First Avenue', 'Ninety-Fifth Street').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State route naming varies; for directional abbreviations see 10.34 and 8.56.

rubrics_metrics.name: Building and apartment numbers as arabic numerals (addresses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Building numbers are written as arabic numerals preceding the street name in addresses; apartment/unit numbers likewise written in numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred mailing forms may differ by postal service; for readability in running text numbers may be spelled out ('One Thousand Lake Shore Drive'). See 6.39 and 10.34.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pluralization of spelled-out numbers and numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Spelled-out numbers form plurals as other nouns; numerals form their plurals by adding 's' (no apostrophe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the twenties and thirties' (spelled-out); 'two 240s and three 238s' (numerals). See 7.5 and 7.15.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas as thousands separators in most English usage
rubrics_metrics.description: For numerals of one thousand or more, commas are used between groups of three digits, counting from the right; commas are not used for figures to the right of the decimal marker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '1,512', '32,987', '4,000,500' but '0.32987'. Commas are not used in page numbers, line numbers, addresses, and years (except years of five digits or more). In scientific writing, commas are often omitted from four-digit numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decimal marker conventions (period in US, comma in many other countries)
rubrics_metrics.description: In US usage a period is used as the decimal marker (decimal point) and commas separate groups of three digits; in many other countries a comma is used as decimal marker and thin fixed spaces separate digit groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: US style '33,333.33' vs French/German style '33 333,33'. English-speaking Canadian practice is shifting toward SI spacing. In US publications, follow US style except in direct quotations or where SI style is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: SI number style: thin fixed spaces for digit grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: SI usage normally uses thin, fixed spaces rather than commas to mark off groups of three digits both to the left and right of the decimal marker; either a decimal point or comma may be used to mark the decimal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '3 426 869' or '0.000 007 250'. In electronic publications a nonbreaking space may be used. Do not use a space for groups of only four digits unless alignment in table columns requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telephone number formatting conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In US/Canada seven-digit numbers are conventionally separated by a hyphen; area code often in parentheses (optional). Alternative style drops parentheses. For international numbers use spaces and include plus sign before country code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples domestic: '(000) 000-0000' or '000-000-0000'. International: '+52 55 0000 0000'. Avoid parentheses in international numbers and avoid ambiguous forms like '+44 (0) 20 ...'. Consult ITU standards or local directories for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratios can be spelled out with 'to' or expressed with colon
rubrics_metrics.description: Ratios composed of whole numbers may generally be expressed using 'to' and spelled out in ordinary text or, where numerals are preferred, a colon may be used as shorthand with no space on either side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a three-to-one ratio', 'a 13-to-2 ratio' or 'a 13:2 ratio'. Ratios may also be expressed as decimal fractions in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbered lists and outline style follow separate rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of numerals (arabic and roman) and letters to distinguish items in lists is governed by list/outline style guidance (see 6.127–32).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to chapter 6 for specifics on nested numbering and lettering conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: En dash for inclusive numbers (ranges)
rubrics_metrics.description: An en dash used between two numbers implies up to and including, or through (e.g., 'pages 75-110', '2000-2009', 'age groups 5-7').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use an en dash if using 'from' or 'between' before the numbers: use 'from 75 to 110' (not 'from 75-110'). Inclusive spelled-out numbers should be joined by 'to', not by an en dash ('participants aged forty-five to forty-nine years'). See 6.78–84 for more on en dash usage.
